title: Disable or Modify Tools: Clear Windows Event Logs
shortTitle: Disable or Modify Tools: Clear Windows Event Logs
summary: Clearing Windows Event Logs removes evidence that has already been written, in contrast to the sibling behaviours that stop collection. The adversary runs a built-in utility, a scripting command, or uses the graphical viewer to delete the contents of the System, Application, or Security log, or deletes the stored log files directly from the directory where Windows keeps them. Because Windows records the act of clearing in the very log being cleared, a single deletion produces a distinctive pair of events: one announcing the clear and one marking the log's new state, with the clear event referencing the account that performed it. The strongest discriminator is context, since backup software and maintenance scripts also clear logs; analysts check whether the clear matches a documented job, whether it happened outside a change window, and whether it was immediately followed by logon, service, or account activity consistent with intrusion.

beginner.definition: Windows keeps logs that record events such as logins and program starts. This technique means an attacker deletes those records. They may empty one log, or remove several at once. They can use a command or the graphical event viewer. The aim is to destroy evidence after they have acted.
beginner.whyItMatters: Once a log is cleared, that history is gone for good, and your timeline has a hole. Investigators cannot show which account logged in or what ran on the machine. Attackers usually clear logs just before they leave, so it is often the last sign you get. Catching the clearing event itself, and keeping copies elsewhere, is how you keep the case alive.
howItWorks: The attacker gains administrator rights on the computer.
They clear one or more logs, such as the Security, System, or Application log.
They may instead delete the log files stored on disk.
Windows makes a record of the clearing, and the log then contains almost nothing.
The attacker may also disable logging so later events are not recorded.
Analysts find an empty log and a large gap, with no history to review.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel night desk where every key handover is written in a ledger. Before leaving, a thief tears out the used pages and drops the book back on the desk. The ledger is still there and looks tidy, but nothing before that moment can be checked. The theft is only noticed days later, when the keys cannot be accounted for.
takeaways: Alert on event log clearing, and record who and which computer did it.
Send log copies to a remote collector so clearing the host loses little.
An empty log plus a gap in forwarding is a strong sign of intrusion.

objectives: Explain how clearing logs differs from the parent technique of disabling a tool.
Describe the tools and interfaces used to clear Windows Event Logs.
Identify the recorded event that marks a log being cleared and who did it.
Explain how to distinguish scheduled maintenance clearing from malicious clearing.
Describe how centralised log collection preserves evidence after a local clear.
